mcqs.q: A Class IV restoration is on the proximal surface of an anterior tooth and:
mcqs.explain: Class IV restorations involve the proximal surface AND the incisal angle of anterior teeth.

mcqs.q: The Class IV composite restoration provides a:
opts: Conservative way to restore fractured/defective/carious anterior teeth
mcqs.explain: Composite gives the dentist a conservative treatment to restore fractured, defective or carious anterior teeth.

mcqs.q: Which assessment is VERY important before a Class IV restoration?
mcqs.explain: Pre-operative assessment of occlusion is very important in Class IV because the incisal angle bears functional load.

mcqs.q: The FIRST step in a Class IV composite restoration is:
mcqs.explain: Shade selection is the first step in composite restoration, performed before the tooth dehydrates.

mcqs.q: Compared with Class III, the Class IV preparation is:
opts: Similar but extended to the incisal angle
mcqs.explain: Class IV preparation is similar to Class III, except that it is extended to involve the incisal angle.

mcqs.q: The three Class IV preparation designs are:
mcqs.explain: Class IV designs are conventional, beveled conventional, and modified.

mcqs.q: The CONVENTIONAL Class IV design is mainly used for:
opts: Large Class IV caries extending into the root
mcqs.explain: The conventional design has minimal clinical Class IV use, reserved for large caries extending onto/into the root.

mcqs.q: The BEVELED CONVENTIONAL design is indicated for:
opts: Large proximal areas that involve the incisal angle
mcqs.explain: The beveled conventional design restores large proximal areas involving the incisal angle, the bevel adding retention.

mcqs.q: The cavosurface bevel in Class IV provides:
opts: Additional retention and more etched enamel surface
mcqs.explain: The cavosurface bevel exposes more enamel rod ends for etching/bonding and provides additional retention.

mcqs.q: The bevel in Class IV is best prepared with a:
mcqs.explain: A flame-shaped diamond bur is used to cut the cavosurface bevel.

mcqs.q: The cavosurface bevel is placed at approximately what angle to the external tooth surface?
mcqs.explain: The bevel is cut at roughly 45° to the external tooth surface.

mcqs.q: The recommended width of the Class IV bevel is:
mcqs.explain: Bevel width is 0.5–2 mm, depending on the tooth structure missing and the retention required.

mcqs.q: The MODIFIED design is indicated for:
opts: Small-to-moderate lesions / minor traumatic enamel fractures
mcqs.explain: The modified design is for small-to-moderate Class IV lesions and minor traumatic injuries with fracture limited to enamel.

mcqs.q: In the MODIFIED design, which part is beveled?
mcqs.explain: The modified design removes the least tooth structure and bevels only the cavosurface margin.

mcqs.q: Primary retention of a Class IV composite is from:
mcqs.explain: Primary retention is achieved by micromechanical bonding (acid-etch + resin).

mcqs.q: Secondary (additional) retention in Class IV can be provided by:
mcqs.explain: Additional retention can be gained with bevels and dovetail extensions.

mcqs.q: A lingual dovetail extension is used infrequently because it:
opts: Is less conservative (removes more tooth structure)
mcqs.explain: A lingual dovetail enhances strength/retention but is less conservative, so it is used only when needed.

mcqs.q: A prerequisite for restoring a Class III/IV proximal lesion is:
opts: A properly contoured matrix band and wedge
mcqs.explain: A properly contoured matrix and wedge are a prerequisite, restoring contour/contact and preventing gingival overhang.

mcqs.q: The wedge in a proximal restoration helps to:
opts: Adapt the matrix gingivally and prevent overhang
mcqs.explain: The wedge adapts the matrix band to the gingival margin, preventing an overhang and helping re-establish contact.

mcqs.q: Composite should be placed and cured:
mcqs.explain: Composite is placed incrementally and each increment is light-cured to ensure adequate polymerization and reduce shrinkage stress.

mcqs.q: The final step after placing a Class IV composite is:
mcqs.explain: After curing, the restoration is finished and polished to contour and smooth the surface.

mcqs.q: A minor traumatic anterior fracture limited to enamel is best restored with which Class IV design?
mcqs.explain: Minor traumatic injuries with fracture limited to enamel are restored with the conservative modified design.

saqs.q: Define a Class IV lesion and how its preparation differs from Class III.
saqs.a: Proximal anterior lesion that involves the incisal angle; preparation is like Class III but extended to the incisal angle.

saqs.q: Name the three Class IV preparation designs.
Describe the cavosurface bevel (instrument, angle, width).
saqs.a: Cut with a flame-shaped diamond bur at ~45° to the surface; width 0.5–2 mm.

saqs.q: Give the primary and secondary retention of a Class IV composite.
saqs.a: Primary = micromechanical bonding; secondary = bevels and dovetail extensions.

saqs.q: What is the modified design used for, and what is beveled?
saqs.a: Small-to-moderate lesions / minor enamel trauma; only the cavosurface margin is beveled.

saqs.q: Why are a matrix band and wedge needed in Class III/IV restorations?
saqs.a: To restore contour and contact and prevent gingival overhang (the wedge adapts the matrix).

saqs.q: Outline the restorative sequence after preparation.
saqs.a: Matrix/wedge → etch → bond → place composite incrementally & cure → finish/polish.
